newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BA plotting more alliances, says rival.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BA plotting more alliances, says rival.

text.p: British longhaul airline Virgin Atlantic Airways accused British Airways Plc on Tuesday of having secret plans to team up with KLM Royal Dutch Airlines and Japan Airlines Co Ltd as part of its globalisation strategy.

Virgin's owner Richard Branson said he had reason to believe BA had outline agreements in place with both KLM and JAL but wanted to secure regulatory approvals for its contested alliance with American Airlines first.
Virgin had already correctly predicted proposed link-ups by BA and American with Spanish carrier Iberia Lineas Aereas de Espana SA, which were announced publicly a month ago, he said.

"Like Iberia, we believe they (BA) have an understanding that once they have got the American deal through they will do similar agreements with JAL and KLM," he told reporters at a company press conference.
There has long been speculation that BA has been looking at teaming up with the Dutch and Japanese airlines to add to its global reach, but the companies routinely decline to comment.
"We never comment on speculation about possible alliances, acquisitions or mergers," said a BA spokesman.

Branson was speaking after meeting with the U.S. House of Representatives Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, which was visiting London to hear local views about the proposed alliance with American.
Under the alliance plans, BA intends to co-ordinate its 244 flights a week to 22 U.S. destinations with American's 238 flights from seven U.S. airports to 12 European destinations.

But Virgin and other rival airlines have all objected to the deal. Branson said he told the U.S. Congress members that BA and American together would control 80 percent of the peak-time take-off and landing slots at London Heathrow for trans-Atlantic traffic and said it would be "the merger from hell."
"Fares will go up and the quality of service will go down if the merger is allowed," he said. "The whole thing is completely unrealistic...They are just far too big to be allowed to get together."
Later BA chief executive Robert Ayling accused Virgin of being "afraid of new competition," in opposing the American alliance.

"Virgin wants to maintain its cosy position at Heathrow, with access denied to (U.S.) airlines such as Continental, US Airways, Delta, TWA and Northwest," Ayling said in a statement after his own meeting this morning with the Congressional committee.

BA and American argue that the deal would lead to lower fares because it would only go ahead if Britain and the U.S. first agreed a new open skies aviation trade pact to open up the market to free competition.
Under the current Bermuda II trade pact only BA, American, United Airlines and Virgin are allowed to use London Heathrow for trans-Atlantic services.
All other airlines have to operate London transatlantic services out of Gatwick, which they say is less popular, particularly for transfer traffic.
"The entry of these (other) airlines will see an inevitable fall in air fares from Heathrow to the USA as competition for business increases," Ayling said.
"But it appears Virgin is afraid of increased competition." Branson retorted: "Virgin welcomes competition, provided it is fair competition.
But Ayling said he remained optimistic that the American deal would get approved by the European and U.S. regulatory authorities.
"I am still very hopeful that it will happen. What we still don't know yet is what precisely will be the final rules in Europe," Ayling told BBC radio.
The key issue centres on access to Heathrow, the world's biggest international airport, where currently only four airlines are permitted to operate transatlantic services.

Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) proposed last December that BA and American should release 168 weekly runway slots at Heathrow -- enough to operate 12 daily return flights -- to give other airlines room to compete.
But the European Commission's Competition Directorate has suggested they should release 350 weekly slots.

Ayling indicated on Tuesday that BA and American might now be prepared to release the 168 slots demanded by the OFT, whereas previously he had said such demands would make it "very difficult to proceed."
"Yes, we think that (number) will allow more competition...It will reduce prices (fares) and increase choice and will give a more dynamic industry here in London," he said on Tuesday.
Having struggled for more than a year to agree terms with the European and U.S. authorities, BA has threatened to abandon the deal if regulatory approvals are not granted before November.

Industry sources said BA has prepared contingency plans should the deal be blocked, including the possibility of completing a looser marketing alliance with American which would fall within the terms of the current Anglo-U.S. aviation trade treaty.

But they said there was now a new mood of optimism at BA that the original deal could survive after all, as political factors come into play. "There seems to be a new political element," said one source on Tuesday.
The next hurdle has to be agreement between the EU and Britain because any concessions would be critical to shaping the British negotiating position at open skies aviation trade talks with the U.S.
The EU Competition Commission is not expected to make a decision before next month, and possibly not before October, following Brussels's summer break.

Meanwhile Virgin's Branson said on Tuesday he might drop his objections if enough slots at Heathrow were given up. "If they are willing to give hundreds of slots ....we will be happy to consider it," he said.

But he later declined to say whether the 350 slots proposed by EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert would be sufficient. "If he (Van Miert) sticks by what we know already about what he has proposed that would be a considerable move forwards," Branson told Reuters.
